newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian T-bills open weaker after employment data.
newsitem.headline: Canadian T-bills open weaker after employment data.

text.p: Canadian T-bills opened weaker in quiet trade on Friday on concerns that Canada's falling unemployment rate may signal unexpectedly high economic growth and a looming rise in interest rates, dealers said.
Statistics Canada reported that the unemployment rate dropped to 9.1 percent in June from 9.5 percent in May.
A Reuters survey of economists had predicted a drop to 9.4 percent in June.
Canada's employment growth increased by 51,500 jobs in June, slightly below May's figure of 61,000 but above market expectations of an increase of 38,800.
"The unemployment numbers are making the bill market nervous," said a trader at a large Canadian bank. "The drop was bigger than expected, and that's having a negative effect on markets."
Canada's three-month when-issued T-bill weakened to yield 3.17 percent from a yield of 3.14 percent at the close on Thursday.
Analysts said a stronger Canadian dollar failed to shield money markets from a more bearish tone.
Canada's dollar opened stronger in heavy trade on Friday at C$1.3689 (US$0.7305) on Canada's strong employment numbers.
The bullish sentiment for the currency is not spilling over into the money market, the trader said.

In other prices, the six-month when-issued T-bill weakened to yield 3.41 percent from a yield of 3.38 at the close on Thursday. The one-year T-bill slipped further to yield 4.04 percent from 3.99 percent on Thursday.
The call loan or overnight lending rate traded at 3.25 percent, in the middle of the Bank of Canada's 3.0-3.5 percent target range.
